analysis.one_liner: Makes state and local governments pay damages when their employees violate someone's constitutional rights.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee until the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would hold state and local governments financially responsible whenever one of their employees, acting on the job, deprives someone of rights protected by the Constitution or federal law. It would apply even when the individual employee cannot be sued personally or believed in good faith that the conduct was legal. Victims could collect compensatory and punitive damages, and with their consent the federal government could sue the government unit directly. The bill never advanced past its referral to a Judiciary subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose constitutional rights are violated by state or local government employees — for example, in police misconduct cases — would gain a way to recover damages from the government employer itself, not just from the individual worker. That matters because individual employees are often shielded from personal liability when they reasonably believed their conduct was lawful, leaving victims with no one to collect from.

how_it_helps.text: Makes any state, county, municipality, or other unit of state or local government liable for an employee's constitutional violations committed under color of law, so victims have a solvent defendant to recover from [S2][S3].

Imposes liability even when the employee is not personally liable or had an objectively reasonable good-faith belief the conduct was legal, closing the gap that currently leaves victims uncompensated [S3].
Allows compensatory damages for the injured party and punitive damages for the injured party, the United States, or both, with no duplicate compensatory awards [S2][S3].
Lets the United States sue the government unit to establish liability, but only with the injured party's consent [S2][S3].
Preserves absolute immunity for conduct entitled to it, and uses the same time limit for filing suits as existing civil rights actions under 42 U.S.C. 1983 [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments — and ultimately their taxpayers or insurers — would pay damages when their employees violate constitutional rights. Government attorneys' offices would face more lawsuits and payout exposure.

drawbacks.text: Strict liability for government employers regardless of good faith would expose cities, counties, and states to substantial new payout obligations for employee misconduct, including cases where the government itself had no way to prevent the violation [S3].

Critics of expanded government liability argue that broad damages exposure can push local governments to raise taxes or cut services, or to over-cautious policies, rather than simply deterring misconduct.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill creates a real remedy for a real gap: today, victims of constitutional violations often cannot recover when the individual employee is protected by good-faith immunity and the government entity escapes liability. The cost is that governments, and their taxpayers, would pay for violations even where no one at the top did anything wrong. How heavy that cost would be depends on details the bill leaves to the courts, so the design is ambitious but not carefully tailored.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its civil rights subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or markup and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers Jr. (D-MI) introduced the Civil Rights Protection Act of 1993 on October 21, 1993 [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Judiciary the same day, and on November 15, 1993, referred to its Subcommittee on Civil and Constitutional Rights [S5].
The bill had no cosponsors [S4], and the record shows no further action, hearing, markup, or vote before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local governments are better off because the bill died: they were never made financially liable for their employees' constitutional violations, and victims of those violations gained no new route to compensation.

for.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its sole sponsor; it drew no cosponsors [S1][S4].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee and its Subcommittee on Civil and Constitutional Rights
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 21, 1993, and the subcommittee referral on November 15, 1993, but took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and the bill had zero cosponsors, so there is no record of where members stood beyond the sponsor's party affiliation.

industries.note: The bill would have made cities, counties, and states pay compensatory and punitive damages when employees violate constitutional rights, even without employee personal liability. Governments resisted creating this exposure, and ordinary taxpayers would ultimately fund the payouts.

The bill would have overridden the shield that lets employees off the hook when they reasonably believed their conduct was lawful, though it preserved absolute immunity. Victims could have recovered from the employer instead.
A new statutory cause of action with damages against deep-pocketed government defendants would have expanded the market for civil rights suits on behalf of victims.
